title: Weekly notes
text: The function quartoutils::weekly_notes() makes it easy to create and edit a weekly notes file. Specifically, if a weekly notes file for the present week does not exist1, quartoutils::weekly_notes() will make this file, using a pre-determined template. If such a file already exists, quartoutils::weekly_notes() simply opens this file for you to edit. The file also automatically gets added to a table of all such files, which is accessible from the “Weekly Notes” landing page of the website. This functionality is demonstrated in the video below.

title: Reading notes
text:
The function quartoutils::make_reading_notes() makes it easy to create and edit a file to jot down reading notes.
Specifically, this function creates a new file in the reading-notes subdirectory of the root, using the file name provided through an argument. If such a file already exists, this function quits with an error. The file also automatically gets added to a table of all such files, which is accessible from the “Reading Notes” landing page of the website. This file is also added to the “reading notes” section of each project landing page; this functionality is demonstrated in the video below.

title: How to create new projects
text:
The function qurtoutils::make_project(projectname = "...") simplifies the process of creating a new project subdirectory. A new directory is created under the projects/ directory, using the name specified in the argument projectname.
The project has the following directory structure:

fs::dir_tree("Semester-Project")

Semester-Project
+-- idea-note1.qmd
\-- index.qmd


The index.qmd file for the project will automatically search for weekly meeting notes and reading notes that have the same projects tag as the name for the newly made project.

title: Transcript Quantification
text:
Preparing today’s lab
Today, we will be using previously published Drosophila melanogaster genome and transcriptome, which were taken from NCBI’s RefSeq database, along with a file containing the names of the genome sequences (these will be Salmon’s “decoys”).
This will include uploading files to the HPC and doing a little bit of file manipulation to prepare everything.

Download the files for today from Blackboard

Drosophila.Genome.fasta
Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta
Drosophila.decoys.txt

Open two terminal windows.
In one of those terminals, log onto the HPC
On the HPC and in your lab folder in scr10, you should (hopefully) have a transcript_quantification folder. If you do not, then make one in your lab folder
Move into the transcript_quantification folder
cd ~/scr10/Biol404L/transcript_quantification
Use pwd to view the PATH to this folder. Make sure to copy this path!
You will use your local terminal (not connected to the HPC) to upload data to the transcript_quantification.
# Local Git Bash: course files found on this computer.
cd ~/Desktop/Guided_DGE_Data/Guided_DGE_Data
scp Drosophila.Genome.fasta Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta Drosophila.decoys.txt etdoan@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:~/scr10/Biol404L/transcript_quantification/
scp works by moving files from a location to another location.
By putting the files from your computer first, scp will copy those files from your computer to the HPC. Later, we will do the reverse.
Once your local terminal says the files have uploaded, you can close it.
In the remote (HPC) terminal, check that the files are there.






TipIn case you get stumped





Use the ls command to view everything in your folder!
ls



You should see all three files there!
Make a new folder for Salmon’s outputs, Salmon_Quant






TipIn case you get stumped





Use the mkdir command to make a new folder!
mkdir Salmon_Quant

title: Transcript Quantification
text:
Preparing the Salmon index
Salmon is a pseudo-alignment tool, which quickly “aligns” your raw reads to a transcriptome. To do make this fast and accurate, Salmon needs the transcriptome formatted in a specific way to facilitate its work. This is called indexing and is a common step for many bioinformatic tools.

To generate the indexed dataset for Salmon, we need to prepare a file with the transcriptome and genome together since we are using the genome as a “decoy” to improve the mRNA quantification. This is easily done with another wonderful terminal command, cat.
cat can either show you everything inside a file or “concatenate” (merge) files together. Today we will merge the genome and transcriptome.






TipHow cat works



cat merges files together in the order that you provide them. This means that every subsequent file is “merged” to the bottom of the prior file(s).
This is really important as Salmon expects the genome (our “decoy”) sequences to be at the bottom of the file. So you just put the transcriptome first followed by the genome and make sure to store the output, using > to a new file.
The command is below to help illustrate this! While we are using just two files, this command will work for any number of files!
cat Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta Drosophila.Genome.fasta > Drosophila.Txm_Gnm.fasta


You can now remove the Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta and Drosophila.Genome.fasta files from the HPC.






TipIn case you get stumped





rm -i Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta Drosophila.Genome.fasta



Now we can prepare to generate the Salmon index. First, load conda and activate the txpt_quant container.
If you do not have the txpt_quant container, refer back to the access-setup-hpc guided lab on how to make new containers and install software.
With your container active, you need to make another job submission script! Go ahead and copy the fastq_trim.sh script and save it as salmon_run.sh.
Inside this script, you will need to remove the exising fastp command, then add the following commands to generate the index that Salmon needs for our Drosophila data.
salmon index \
     -p 8 \
     -d Drosophila.decoys.txt \
     -i dmel_index \
     -t Drosophila.Txm_Gnm.fasta
Here is a breakdown of the command:

index: tells Salmon that we are preparing its index
-p: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as --ntasks)
-d: PATH to the decoys.txt file (these are just the name of the genome sequences)
-i: what you would like Salmon to name your index
-t: PATH to the merge transcriptome and genome fasta files

All you need to do now is submit the job submission script!






TipIn case you get stumped





sbatch salmon_run.sh

title: Transcript Quantification
text:
Quantify Transcript Abundance!
With the index prepared, it is fairly easy to start quantifying transcript abundance from each of the trimmed reads, which were prepared before.

First, let’s update the existing salmon_run.sh file. This time instead of deleting the command, let’s leave it there. However, add one # in front of each line in the command to “comment out” the command. This will prevent it from being run each time this script is submitted.
This is a nice way to leave useful bits of code in these job submission scripts that we use rarely. It can serve as a nice reference for later!
Now add the command to run the quantification to the salmon_run.sh script.
salmon quant -i dmel_index \
   -l A \
   -1 ../raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Fwd.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
   -2 ../raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Rev.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
   -p 8 \
   -o Salmon_Quant/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1_Quant
Here is a breakdown of the command:

quant: tells Salmon that we are quantifying transcript expression
-i: PATH to the Salmon index
-l: specify what type of sequencing library we used (A tells Salmon to determine this automatically)
-1: PATH to the forward reads
-2: PATH to the reverse reads
-p: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as --ntasks)
-o: what you would like Salmon to name the output directories it is going to make

There are some placeholder names that you can update!







Caution



The steps below are to show you how to run the transcript quantification with just one set of trimmed reads.
You will need to update the names as appropriate.
This can be automated a bit more, but I want to stress that being pushed to touch and update these files repeatedly will help it become more familiar and easy to do!



For each of the sets of reads, it would be best to provide the full path to the trimmed reads in the script. Especially, as you should be working in your transcript_quantification folder, we do not have to any confusing navigation.
The paths below use my scr10 directory on the HPC.
salmon quant \
     -i dmel_index \
     -l A \
     -1 ~/scr10/Biol404L/raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Fwd.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -2 ~/scr10/Biol404L/raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Rev.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -p 8 \
     -o Salmon_Quant/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1_Quant
You can see that I added the sample information to the -o to make it clear which set of trimmed reads were being processed.
Submit the salmon_run.sh script and feel free to update it with new sets of reads and repeat!
Sit back and rest for a moment! We are finally about to touch some results! Yay!

Downloading the Salmon quantification files
We will be using R-Studio for a brief moment, before downloading the output transcript-level quantification files from Salmon

With R-Studio open, go to the File menu and select New Project
In the pop-up menu select New Directory
Then choose New Project and name the new directory Guided_DGE_Analysis
When prompted, use the menu to put this project as a sub-directory of your Desltop
You should see the Guided_DGE_Analysis on your Desktop
Inside that folder, make the following new folders

quant_data
metadata
results

Open a new local terminal and move into quant_data folder inside the Guided_DGE_Analysis folder






TipIn case you get stumped





cd ~/Desktop/Guided_DGE_Analysis/quant_data



Once inside your quant_data, we can download ALL of the Salmon outputs. Each sample will be in its own folder. To make it easy, get the PATH, using pwd, to the Salmon_Quant folder on the HPC.
**Make sure you are in the quant_data folder before continuing!
When ready, we will use scp to download the data from the HPC to our quant_data folder locally.
In your local terminal, use scp to download the data.
scp -r "etdoan@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:~/scr10/Biol404L/transcript_quantification/Salmon_Quant/Dmel*" .






TipFor Mac Users





Sometimes the terminal hates the wildcard character, *. To force it to use it in a way that makes sense, you just need to slightly adjust the scp command
scp -r "etdoan@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:~/scr10/Biol404L/transcript_quantification/Salmon_Quant/Dmel*" .

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Before we get started
All of the labs for this course will be in QuartoMD format like this. You will be required to copy these to your own personal account and should be updating them! Your only formal grades for this course are based on the semester project. These guided-labs are there to help you build your familiarity with creating documentation, managing, data, reporting, and with all sorts of coding and scripting.
Update and add things as you see fit! The more effort you place here, the more useful this will be for you!
At times, I will include blocks to highlight snippets of code and/or get you to pause and think!






NoteNote



There will be some questions in blue that you can answer.


Some commands/instructions will have the potential to set you back, and require some deeper thought and/or carefulness.






CautionCaution



This will highlight things that may need a bit of caution before you proceed.
This can include steps that may take a bit of time, or dangerous coding commands (e.g., those that remove all the files…)








WarningWarning



Sometimes, it may just be a simple ‘warning’.


The first few weeks of the lab will focus on getting you comfortable with the command-line, before we move into diverse analyses, including differential gene expression and population genomics. This will include step-by-step instructions using our examplar data sets.
My goal is for you to feel comfortable enough to repeat the analyses on the data set of your choice!

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
W&M’s HPC server
If you are using your own computer and want to access the HPC from off-campus, then you will need to download the W&M VPN client. See this vpn installation link for instructions. If you are connected to the W&M Wi-Fi you will not need to connect to the VPN.
Once you are conneced to the W&M VPN, or using the W&M Wi-Fi, you will need to ssh into one of the sciclone’s subclusters. SciClone is comprised of many different servers (subclusters), each with their own unique set of resources (i.e., high powered CPU’s but low RAM). For most of the lab, we will be using bora.
If using your own computer and you run into issues accessing the HPC, ask me for help if needed!

Overview of the UNIX operating system and directory structure

The core structure of Unix directories follows a hierarchical tree-like organization. The root directory serves as the top-level directory, and all other directories and files are organized beneath it
When you first connect to the server, you will be in your home directory by default.
Keep this structure in mind when you’re navigating through directories, especially once we start up/downloading data to your personal computers.
If you ever get confused where you are you can return to the home directory using cd

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Connecting to bora.sciclone.wm.edu
For both PCs and Macs, I recommend using the terminal to access SciClone.

Open the Terminal software
Connect to the remote server using ssh with your username:






NoteSSH into Bora



My W&M username is etdoan.
ssh etdoan@bora.sciclone.wm.edu


When you connect, you will be sitting in your home directory on the HPC!

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
HPC Navigation
Moving around the HPC uses common UNIX commands (I will provide a link to a useful cheatsheet).
When you first log in, you are interacting the HPC’s head-node (we will talk about this in class!). Additionally, the location where you first “land” onto the HPC is not where you will work!
Before we do too much, let’s use some basic commands to see what is in our current folder, move around, and check where we are:

It may be kind of weird to think like this, but the parts of your laptop that you interact with really are just graphical representations of folders (directories). This is no different on the HPC! We can see the contents of this directory really easily.
ls
You should see a couple big directories, including scr10, scr20, scr30. These are the “scratch” spaces, which is our playground!






CautionStorage Limitations



Do not store files outside of scr10 for this lab. Additionally, do not use scr10 as a semi-permanent storage space! It is purged every few months, so please treat it like a shared kitchen and make sure we clean up after ourselves when we can!


Let’s move into scr10, which is where we will do most of our work
cd scr10
It can be easy to get lost on the HPC! Thankfully, we have the best unix command ever: pwd
pwd






Notepwd is your Friend!



The output of pwd is the PATH to your current location. Each / marks a different directory, so you can see exactly where you are.
This is referred to as the absolute PATH, which is just like having exact GPS coordinates for where you are!


If you ever get lost, and this will happen, simply using cd will bring you back to your home directory
While we are here, let’s make a folder the lab too
mkdir Biol404L
Move into the new folder you made!






TipIn case you get stumped





Use the cd command to move into your folder!
cd Biol404L



Use ls and pwd to see what is inside this folder and where you are on the HPC!
Move back to your home directory






TipIn case you get stumped





Use the cd by itself to move to your home directory!
cd



Soon we will be done moving around for a little bit, just a few more to do! Let’s move directly into our Biol404L directory, then use pwd to check!
cd scr10/Biol404L
pwd
You made it!
We can also move “backwards” to a less “nested” folder. We can use .. to navigate back a directory relative to where we are. Let’s try it out and see what it looks like!
cd ..
pwd
Move back into your Biol404L folder (see the prior commands/steps if you need help, before asking me or a neighbor)
Let’s move “backwards” two times at once!
cd ../..






NoteDid you notice?





To move back one directory, we use ... However, to move back two directories, we have to put a ‘/’ in the middle!
You can do this as many times as needed, although it can get confusing…



Where are you now? How would you check?
If you feel comfortable, make sure to move back into the Biol404L folder.
One last task before we continue! Make a new directory called Slurm_Scripts then move into it!






TipIn case you get stumped





You can use the mkdir command!
mkdir Slurm_Scripts
cd Slurm_Scripts




Great! You are now on your way to becoming a UNIX navigation expert.

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Dealing with Containers
This next section will combine a fair bit of commands, which will become more familiar as you work in this lab. You are not expected to be an expert right away!

Loading Modules (Software)
The HPC has quite a lot of software already installed on it. This varies by with subclusters you are working with (remember we are working on bora).






NoteWant to see the available software





If you do, then run the following command:
module avail



We do want to use containers in this lab. To do so, we will be using Anaconda and BioConda.

Load the miniforge module
module load miniforge3/24.9.2-0
Let’s see what modules are loaded already
module avail






NoteWhat do you see?





You should notice that two pieces of software are highlighted!
SLURM and Miniforge3!



Miniforge3 is our Anaconda software. However, it does not natively connect or know where to find bioinformatic packages. Most of those are available through BioConda.
We will follow the BioConda setup instructions for Conda that are found on their website.
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict

Now we are almost ready to install software! Woohoo!
It is worth noting that conda refers to their “containers” as environments. For our purposes, this is the same thing, so do not be alarmed!

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Submitting HPC Jobs
In this part we will set up a job submission script. These are important to understand as we will be using them throughout the lab course.
I have placed a template of one below (I will break down what each part means!):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=some-job-name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH -t 1:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G
It is nice to keep your job submission scripts together, staying organized is KEY!


Making our first job-submission-script
We will actually be submitting a job to make our container and install some software! The easiest option is to use an existing text editor in the terminal, pico

Open a new file, prep_conda_env.sh, with pico Your screen should be empty!
Copy and paste the template for our job submission that was found in the last section
To “write” the file quickly (equivalent of saving), press ctl+o keys at the same time and hit enter
Now, using your arrow keys, please replace some-job-name with env-prep and “write” the file again
Great, we are ready to add our command! We will create a new environment, called sra_prep. In it we will install several pieces of software:

sra-tools: this makes it easy to download raw data from NCBI’s SRA repository
ncbi-datasets-cli: makes it easy to access genomes from NCBI’s GenBank and RefSeq
parallel-fastq-dump: speeds up the initial unpacking of SRA data
fastp: quality trimming tool (also provides lovely QC outputs!)

Add the following to your script:
conda create -n sra_prep ncbi-datasets-cli sra-tools parallel-fastq-dump fastp -y
Make sure to save!
Check your script (below)






TipWorking Submission Script





#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=some-job-name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH -t 1:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G

conda create -n sra_prep ncbi-datasets-cli sra-tools fastp parallel-fastq-dump -y



Exit the pico editor with ctl+x
Submitting the job to run is incredibly easy! You will just use sbatch
sbatch prep_conda_env.sh
Now we wait… You can track the progress in the queue!
squeue --m
Above will show only your jobs, whereas the code below will show *all the jobs
squeue
Once this is finished, you will need to make one more container! Updating the prep_conda_env.sh script, you will need to:


create a new container called txpt_quant
install salmon
install star

Make sure this is run before we meet next!

Once your job is finished, activate your container!
conda activate sra_prep
If it works, you will see (sra_prep) on the left-hand side of the terminal!
Look at the fastp help message and all its options (so many)
fastp -h
Using -h with most tools will bring up usage information along with all their options. It is a lazy nice way to make to sure that the software is installed!
To exit the HPC, simply press ctl+d at the same time! You should see something like: Connection to bora.sciclone.wm.edu closed.

Disconnecting from the HPC is safe to do any time that a job is running or queued!
In fact, that is the advantage of the HPC! You can queue some work then do something else (nap, eat some cookies, compose a bioinformatics sonnet, etc)
You made it! Huzzah!

title: Working with GitHub
section: Setting up and managing your GitHub!
text:
Setting up and managing your GitHub!
We are going to first “clone” the repository you made by hand. Afterwards, we will add some files to it, upload it back to GitHub with those new files (yay backups), and setup your lab notebook webpage!

Download your empty lab reposity from GitHub (only need to do this the first day)
git clone https://github.com/EthanDoan0517/Bio404L.git
Download the files from BlackBoard and put them into the empty repository on your computer
Using your terminal (or git-bash), move into this folder on your computer.
Render them quickly using R-Studio (or the terminal)
Check if you have local updates that are not found in the remote repository

title: Working with SRA Data
text:
Downloading SRA datasets
You will need to make a copy of your job submission script that you created during last week’s lab, which you can then edit to make it easy to download and process your raw read downloads!

Make sure you are in the raw_read_prep folder






TipIn case you get stumped

Make a copy of last week’s slurm script and rename it sra_download.sh
cp ../Slurm_Scripts/prep_conda_env.sh ../Slurm_Scripts/sra_download.sh
Did you notice that the above command uses relative paths to copy (cp) the file!
You need to edit the contents of the new sra_download.sh file! Use nano to start editing the file






TipIn case you get stumped





nano ../Slurm_Scripts/sra_download.sh



We will start by making a for loop using bash to download three of the sequencing runs. You will be using prefetch to download the data. prefetch is part of the sratools suite of tools that NCBI has released to make it easier to access raw sequencing data from the SRA repository.
Make sure to delete the existing command inside the file. Then add the following for loop.
for seqrun in SRR1576457 SRR1576458 SRR1576459
do

done
Make sure to update the job-name! And this may take a little bit of time, so do not be alarmed!
Submit your job!

squeue --m

title: Working with SRA Data
text:
Unpacking SRA datasets
If you were curious and used ls to peek into those newly created folders, you would have seen a file ending in .sra. This is the packed (compressed) raw data!
We need to unpack it using the tool parallel-fastq-dump.
Below, is a walkthrough of one way to do this. It is a bit involved, but it will make it easy to link the file to the existing metadata!
You should repeat the following steps for each file

Make a copy of last week’s slurm script and rename it sra_fastq_dump.sh
cp ../Slurm_Scripts/prep_conda_env.sh ../Slurm_Scripts/sra_fastq_dump.sh
Make some extra edits to this file!

update the job-name
update the --ntasks value to 8
delete the old command

Now we will add the command to run parallel-fastq-dump
parallel-fastq-dump --split-files \
     --gzip \
     --threads 8 \
     -s SRR1576457 \
     -O Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1
Here is a breakdown of the command:

--split-files: separate the file into forward and reverse reads (the data are paired-end!)
--gzip: these raw fastq files can be big, so we will keep them compressed
--threads 8: tells the HPC to multi-task on this job, splitting the job into 8 pieces to speed it up
-s SRR#: tells the tool which dataset we want to process
-O NAME: the name we want the output folder to be. It is typically nice to include the metadata and/or the SRR accession (or both)

Using sbatch, submit the job!
Repeat for the other datasets that have FINISHED downloading. Use squeue --m to check that the files you are trying to unpack have finished downloading!
As before, it is up to you to unpack the rest of the datasets during our time in lab (or outside if that’s easier). So long as one of the sequencing runs is downloaded and unpacked, you can move on to the last section, which is trimming and the quality checking!

title: Working with SRA Data
text:
Trimming raw SRA datasets
If you were curious and used ls to peek into those newly created folders, you would have seen a file ending in .sra. This is the packed (compressed) raw data!
We need to unpack it using the tool parallel-fastq-dump.
Below, is a walkthrough of one way to do this. It is a bit involved, but it will make it easy to link the file to the existing metadata!
You should repeat the following steps for each file

Make a copy of the sra_fastq_dump.sh slurm script and rename it fastq_trim.sh






TipIn case you get stumped





cp ../Slurm_Scripts/prep_conda_env.sh ../Slurm_Scripts/sra_fastq_trim.sh



You will need to edit the newly copied script, sra_fastq_trim.sh. As the prior script already was set up for multi-threading (--ntasks=8), the only change is to replace the prior command with one for our read-trimming tool, fastp.
The command is below, followed by a breakdown of the options. The below command is written for just one file, so you will need to adjust this!
fastp \
     -i Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1/SRR1576457_1.fastq.gz \
     -I Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1/SRR1576457_2.fastq.gz \
     -o Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Fwd.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -O Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Rev.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -h Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.html \
     -R "Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1 Report" \
     -q 20  \
     -l 80 \
     -w 8 \
     -r
Here is a breakdown of the command:

-i: PATH to your forward reads
-I: PATH to your reverse reads
-o: what to name your trimmed forward reads
-O: what to name your trimmed reverse reads
-h: what to name the output quality score html file
-R: the report name to add to the output quality score html file
-q: minimum Phred quality score to use for read trimming
-l: minimum read length to keep a read following trimming
-w: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as --ntasks)
-r: perform the per-base trimming starting on the right side of the read

Using sbatch, submit the job!
Repeat for the other datasets that have FINISHED unpacking with parallel-fastq-dump. Use squeue --m to check that the files you are trying to unpack have finished downloading!

title: Working with SRA Data
text:
Cleaning up after ourselves
By now, you will have tons of files, all sitting inside your raw_read_prep folder. We do need to make sure to clean-up after ourselves on the HPC, as we have many “intermediate” files, which take up a reasonably large amount of space.
To do our cleanup, we will be using a dangerous command, rm. What makes this command so dangerous is that it removes the files/folders permanently. This is like moving a file to your trash on your computer and tossing the trash out at the same time.
Take your time when doing this! We will remove files little bit by little bit.

Running and submitting jobs to SLURM will generate a ton of “slurm.out” files. These are logs from the HPC and the tool(s) you used. Typically, you won’t need these for very long, outside of handling errors.
We can remove all of these in one step!






WarningRemoving slurm logs



rm slurm-*.out


rm followed by a file, will remove the file. You can also use the wildcard character, *. In the example above, the way this is put in the command effectively tells the computer “remove anything that startswith slurm- and ends with .out”
Make sure to remove all the files that end with .json as we do not need these!






WarningRemoving slurm logs



rm *.json


This step is for any sequencing runs that have been fully processed, which includes downloading, unpacking, trimming. We will start by removing each of the intermediate folders, one at a time. It is okay to do this slowly and carefully, as you don’t want to need to do the processing over again.
Below is the command to remove just one of the folders from the initial SRR downloading






WarningRemoving Folders



rm -rf SRR1576457


You can combine this with the wildcard to remove all of the SRR folders, but you need to be very certain you have “unpacked” them!
You can also use that command to remove any folders, but again, please be cautious!

title: Transcript Quantification
text:
Preparing today’s lab
Today, we will be using previously published Drosophila melanogaster genome and transcriptome, which were taken from NCBI’s RefSeq database, along with a file containing the names of the genome sequences (these will be Salmon’s “decoys”).
This will include uploading files to the HPC and doing a little bit of file manipulation to prepare everything.

Download the files for today from Blackboard

Drosophila.Genome.fasta
Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta
Drosophila.decoys.txt

Open two terminal windows.
In one of those terminals, log onto the HPC
On the HPC and in your lab folder in scr10, you should (hopefully) have a transcript_quantification folder. If you do not, then make one in your lab folder
Move into the transcript_quantification folder
cd ~/scr10/Biol404L/transcript_quantification
Use pwd to view the PATH to this folder. Make sure to copy this path!
You will use your local terminal (not connected to the HPC) to upload data to the transcript_quantification.
# Local Git Bash: course files found on this computer.
cd ~/Desktop/Guided_DGE_Data/Guided_DGE_Data
scp Drosophila.Genome.fasta Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta Drosophila.decoys.txt etdoan@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:~/scr10/Biol404L/transcript_quantification/
scp works by moving files from a location to another location.
By putting the files from your computer first, scp will copy those files from your computer to the HPC. Later, we will do the reverse.
Once your local terminal says the files have uploaded, you can close it.
In the remote (HPC) terminal, check that the files are there.






TipIn case you get stumped





Use the ls command to view everything in your folder!
ls



You should see all three files there!
Make a new folder for Salmon’s outputs, Salmon_Quant






TipIn case you get stumped





Use the mkdir command to make a new folder!
mkdir Salmon_Quant

title: Transcript Quantification
text:
Preparing the Salmon index
Salmon is a pseudo-alignment tool, which quickly “aligns” your raw reads to a transcriptome. To do make this fast and accurate, Salmon needs the transcriptome formatted in a specific way to facilitate its work. This is called indexing and is a common step for many bioinformatic tools.

To generate the indexed dataset for Salmon, we need to prepare a file with the transcriptome and genome together since we are using the genome as a “decoy” to improve the mRNA quantification. This is easily done with another wonderful terminal command, cat.
cat can either show you everything inside a file or “concatenate” (merge) files together. Today we will merge the genome and transcriptome.






TipHow cat works



cat merges files together in the order that you provide them. This means that every subsequent file is “merged” to the bottom of the prior file(s).
This is really important as Salmon expects the genome (our “decoy”) sequences to be at the bottom of the file. So you just put the transcriptome first followed by the genome and make sure to store the output, using > to a new file.
The command is below to help illustrate this! While we are using just two files, this command will work for any number of files!
cat Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta Drosophila.Genome.fasta > Drosophila.Txm_Gnm.fasta


You can now remove the Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta and Drosophila.Genome.fasta files from the HPC.






TipIn case you get stumped





rm -i Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta Drosophila.Genome.fasta



Now we can prepare to generate the Salmon index. First, load conda and activate the txpt_quant container.
If you do not have the txpt_quant container, refer back to the access-setup-hpc guided lab on how to make new containers and install software.
With your container active, you need to make another job submission script! Go ahead and copy the fastq_trim.sh script and save it as salmon_run.sh.
Inside this script, you will need to remove the exising fastp command, then add the following commands to generate the index that Salmon needs for our Drosophila data.
salmon index \
     -p 8 \
     -d Drosophila.decoys.txt \
     -i dmel_index \
     -t Drosophila.Txm_Gnm.fasta
Here is a breakdown of the command:

index: tells Salmon that we are preparing its index
-p: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as --ntasks)
-d: PATH to the decoys.txt file (these are just the name of the genome sequences)
-i: what you would like Salmon to name your index
-t: PATH to the merge transcriptome and genome fasta files

All you need to do now is submit the job submission script!






TipIn case you get stumped





sbatch salmon_run.sh

title: Transcript Quantification
text:
Quantify Transcript Abundance!
With the index prepared, it is fairly easy to start quantifying transcript abundance from each of the trimmed reads, which were prepared before.

First, let’s update the existing salmon_run.sh file. This time instead of deleting the command, let’s leave it there. However, add one # in front of each line in the command to “comment out” the command. This will prevent it from being run each time this script is submitted.
This is a nice way to leave useful bits of code in these job submission scripts that we use rarely. It can serve as a nice reference for later!
Now add the command to run the quantification to the salmon_run.sh script.
salmon quant -i dmel_index \
   -l A \
   -1 ../raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Fwd.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
   -2 ../raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Rev.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
   -p 8 \
   -o Salmon_Quant/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1_Quant
Here is a breakdown of the command:

quant: tells Salmon that we are quantifying transcript expression
-i: PATH to the Salmon index
-l: specify what type of sequencing library we used (A tells Salmon to determine this automatically)
-1: PATH to the forward reads
-2: PATH to the reverse reads
-p: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as --ntasks)
-o: what you would like Salmon to name the output directories it is going to make

There are some placeholder names that you can update!







Caution



The steps below are to show you how to run the transcript quantification with just one set of trimmed reads.
You will need to update the names as appropriate.
This can be automated a bit more, but I want to stress that being pushed to touch and update these files repeatedly will help it become more familiar and easy to do!



For each of the sets of reads, it would be best to provide the full path to the trimmed reads in the script. Especially, as you should be working in your transcript_quantification folder, we do not have to any confusing navigation.
The paths below use my scr10 directory on the HPC.
salmon quant \
     -i dmel_index \
     -l A \
     -1 ~/scr10/Biol404L/raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Fwd.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -2 ~/scr10/Biol404L/raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Rev.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -p 8 \
     -o Salmon_Quant/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1_Quant
You can see that I added the sample information to the -o to make it clear which set of trimmed reads were being processed.
Submit the salmon_run.sh script and feel free to update it with new sets of reads and repeat!
Sit back and rest for a moment! We are finally about to touch some results! Yay!

title: Four guided labs: completion audit
text:
Panama processing problems identified
The saved Dmel_Panama_29C_Rep1.html report names input accession SRR1576466; the metadata requires SRR1576514. The Rep2 report names SRR1576467; the metadata requires SRR1576515. Thus, those filenames do not establish that the required samples were processed.
Both reports show mean input read lengths of 76 bases and a command using fastp -l 80. More than 99.8% of reads were rejected as too short, with zero reads retained. Before rerunning, verify the correct accessions and their read lengths against the course metadata. Changing the length cutoff alone would not resolve the sample mismatch.

Compare saved local products with HPC products and copy any genuinely missing completed outputs.
